# Story 1.1: Enrol an authenticator app
Status: ready-for-dev

## Story
As an account holder, I want to enrol an authenticator app by scanning a QR code and confirming one generated code, so that I can protect my sign-in with a time-based one-time password.

## Acceptance Criteria
- AC-1: Given a signed-in user without 2FA, when they start enrolment, then a QR code for a new authenticator secret is shown.
- AC-2: Given an enrolment in progress, when they submit the code currently generated by their app, then enrolment completes and the account shows 2FA as enabled.
- AC-3: Given an enrolment in progress, when they submit an incorrect code, then enrolment does not complete and the account still shows 2FA as disabled.

## Tasks / Subtasks
- [ ] Generate a TOTP secret and render it as a QR code on the enrolment page (AC: 1)
- [ ] Keep the candidate secret in the session until a code is confirmed (AC: 1, 3)
- [ ] Verify the submitted code against the candidate secret with pyotp (AC: 2, 3)
- [ ] On successful confirmation, write the secret to `totp_secret` on the users table and mark 2FA enabled (AC: 2)
- [ ] On a wrong code, show an error and leave `totp_secret` unset (AC: 3)

## Dev Notes
- FR-1 is the requirement behind this story. Enrolment completes only after one generated code is confirmed.
- Architecture: `totp_secret` is added to the users table, and TOTP verification uses pyotp with no new service. The secret is not persisted until confirmation.

- [Source: docs/architecture.md#data-model]
- [Source: docs/architecture.md#verification]

# Story 1.2: Require a TOTP code at sign-in
Status: ready-for-dev

## Story
As an account holder with 2FA enabled, I want sign-in to require a valid TOTP code after my password, so that a stolen password alone is not enough to get into my account.

## Acceptance Criteria
- AC-1: Given a 2FA-enabled account, when the user submits the correct password, then they see a TOTP code prompt and are not yet signed in.
- AC-2: Given the TOTP code prompt, when the user submits the code currently generated by their app, then they are signed in.
- AC-3: Given the TOTP code prompt, when the user submits an invalid code, then they are not signed in and see an error.
- AC-4: Given an account without 2FA, when the user submits the correct password, then they are signed in without a code prompt.

## Tasks / Subtasks
- [ ] After the password step, send 2FA-enabled users to a TOTP code prompt before any session is created (AC: 1, 4)
- [ ] Verify the submitted code against the user's `totp_secret` with pyotp (AC: 2, 3)
- [ ] Create the signed-in session only after a valid code is accepted (AC: 2, 3)
- [ ] Show an error on the TOTP prompt when the code is invalid (AC: 3)
- [ ] Keep the existing password-only sign-in path for accounts without 2FA (AC: 4)

## Dev Notes
- FR-2 is the requirement behind this story. Sign-in for a 2FA-enabled account requires a valid TOTP code after the password step.
- Architecture: the TOTP check uses pyotp against `totp_secret` on the users table, with no new service.

### References
- [Source: docs/prd.md#FR-2]
- [Source: docs/architecture.md#data-model]
- [Source: docs/architecture.md#verification]

# Story 1.3: Issue recovery codes at enrolment
Status: ready-for-dev

## Story
As an account holder, I want ten single-use recovery codes issued when I finish enrolling, so that I can recover access if I lose my device.

## Acceptance Criteria
- AC-1: Given an enrolment that has just been confirmed, when the enrolment completes, then the user is shown exactly ten recovery codes.
- AC-2: Given the ten recovery codes shown at enrolment, when the user reads them, then all ten are distinct.
- AC-3: Given an enrolment whose confirmation code is wrong, when the user is shown the result, then no recovery codes are shown and none are stored.

## Tasks / Subtasks
- [ ] Generate ten distinct recovery codes when enrolment is confirmed (AC: 1, 2)
- [ ] Store the codes in `recovery_codes` on the users table in the same step that writes `totp_secret` (AC: 1, 3)
- [ ] Display the ten codes on the enrolment completion page (AC: 1, 2)
- [ ] Generate and store no codes when confirmation fails (AC: 3)

## Dev Notes
- FR-3 is the requirement behind this story. Ten single-use recovery codes are issued at enrolment.
- Architecture: `recovery_codes` is added to the users table alongside `totp_secret`.

### References
- [Source: docs/prd.md#FR-3]
- [Source: docs/architecture.md#data-model]

# Story 1.4: Sign in with a recovery code
Status: ready-for-dev

## Story
As an account holder who has lost their device, I want to sign in with one of my recovery codes in place of a TOTP code, so that I can regain access to my account.

## Acceptance Criteria
- AC-1: Given the TOTP code prompt, when the user submits an unused recovery code, then they are signed in.
- AC-2: Given a recovery code that has already been used, when the user submits it again, then they are not signed in and see an error.
- AC-3: Given a recovery code that has already been used, when the user signs in with a different unused recovery code, then they are signed in.
- AC-4: Given the TOTP code prompt, when the user submits a value that matches no remaining recovery code, then they are not signed in and see an error.

## Tasks / Subtasks
- [ ] Accept a recovery code on the TOTP code prompt as an alternative to a TOTP code (AC: 1, 4)
- [ ] Sign the user in when the submitted value matches an unused code in `recovery_codes` (AC: 1, 3)
- [ ] Remove a recovery code from `recovery_codes` as soon as it is used, so it cannot be reused (AC: 2, 3)
- [ ] Refuse any value that matches no remaining code and show an error (AC: 4)

## Dev Notes
- FR-3 is the requirement behind this story. Any one recovery code can replace a TOTP code, once.
- Architecture: recovery codes are read from and removed from `recovery_codes` on the users table; the check runs in the same sign-in step as TOTP verification.

### References
- [Source: docs/prd.md#FR-3]
- [Source: docs/architecture.md#data-model]
- [Source: docs/architecture.md#verification]

FR-3 is split into 1.3 (issuance) and 1.4 (redemption) because a user notices those as two separate outcomes. The architecture does not say whether `recovery_codes` are stored hashed or in plain text; that needs a decision before 1.3 is built.

   demonstrated. A story is a thing a user can do, or a property they can observe, end to end.

4. **One story per requirement is the default.** Split further only when a requirement
   contains two outcomes a user would notice separately. Merge only when two requirements
   describe one outcome. Do not add setup stories: configuring a dependency is a task inside
   the story that needs it.

5. **Acceptance criteria state observable outcomes.** "Then the behaviour is covered by a
   test" asserts nothing about the product. Name what the user or the caller sees.

6. **Close the task-to-criterion mapping.** Every task carries `(AC: n)`, every referenced
   criterion exists, and every criterion is covered by at least one task.

7. **References must resolve.** Cite only the source files named in the input, with an anchor
   that exists in them.

Mention the requirement id in Dev Notes as plain text, e.g. `FR-2 is the requirement behind
this story.` — the linter looks for it there.

# Story 1.1: Reject over-limit requests with 429 and Retry-After
Status: ready-for-dev

## Story
As an API consumer, I want a request over my key's limit to be rejected with 429 and a Retry-After header, so that I know when to try again.

## Acceptance Criteria
- AC-1: Given an API key that has reached its per-key limit, when it sends another request, then the response status is 429 Too Many Requests.
- AC-2: Given a 429 response, when the client reads the response headers, then Retry-After gives the time at which the key's limit next allows a request.
- AC-3: Given an API key that is under its per-key limit, when it sends a request, then the request is served and not rejected.

## Tasks / Subtasks
- [ ] Count each API key's requests in the Redis counter store per limit window (AC: 1, 3)
- [ ] Reject a request over the key's limit with 429 before the endpoint handler runs (AC: 1)
- [ ] Set Retry-After on every 429 to the time the key's limit next allows a request (AC: 2)
- [ ] Serve requests under the limit without change to their response (AC: 3)

## Dev Notes
- FR-1 is the requirement behind this story.
- Counters live in Redis, the intended counter store, not in process memory (see counter-store).
- The per-key limit is read from the existing `api_keys` table (see data-model), so the lookup is keyed by API key.

# Story 1.2: Give an API key a custom limit that overrides the default
Status: ready-for-dev

## Story
As an integration partner, I want my API key to have a custom limit that overrides the default, so that my existing burst traffic keeps working unchanged.

## Acceptance Criteria
- AC-1: Given an API key with a custom limit set, when it sends requests, then it is rejected with 429 only after exceeding that custom limit, not the default limit.
- AC-2: Given an API key with no custom limit set, when it sends requests, then the default limit applies and its behaviour is unchanged from before the limit column existed.
- AC-3: Given the two existing integration partners' keys have custom limits set, when they send their current traffic, then none of their requests receive a 429.

## Tasks / Subtasks
- [ ] Add a nullable limit column to the `api_keys` table so existing rows keep the default (AC: 2)
- [ ] Apply a key's custom limit in place of the default when the column is set (AC: 1)
- [ ] Fall back to the default limit when the column is null (AC: 2)
- [ ] Set custom limits on the two existing partner keys to cover their current traffic (AC: 3)

## Dev Notes
- FR-2 is the requirement behind this story.
- The limit is read from `api_keys`, which has no limit column yet (see data-model), so the column is added here as nullable; null means the default applies.

### References
- [Source: docs/prd.md#FR-2]
- [Source: docs/architecture.md#data-model]

# Story 1.3: Rate-limit counters survive an application restart
Status: ready-for-dev

## Story
As an API consumer, I want my rate-limit budget to survive an application restart, so that a restart does not hand me a fresh budget.

## Acceptance Criteria
- AC-1: Given an API key has used part of its budget, when the application restarts, then its next request is counted from where it left off, not from zero.
- AC-2: Given an API key is at its limit, when the application restarts, then its next request still receives a 429 with a Retry-After that reflects the original window.

## Tasks / Subtasks
- [ ] Hold rate-limit counters in the Redis counter store instead of process memory (AC: 1, 2)
- [ ] Key each counter by API key so the application finds it again after a restart (AC: 1, 2)
- [ ] Give each counter an expiry matching its window so Retry-After is computed from stored state (AC: 2)
- [ ] Add an integration test that restarts the application against Redis and checks the counter carries over (AC: 1, 2)

## Dev Notes
- CAP-1 is the requirement behind this story.
- Redis is already in the stack and is the intended counter store (see counter-store); in-process counters would reset on restart.
